note.text: An argumentative essay defends a position through reasons. A claim needs support that bears on it; repeating a preference is not evidence. A counterargument presents a relevant objection, and a response explains how the writer addresses it. A conclusion should follow the discussion rather than introduce an unsupported new case. An argument can be firm without insulting opponents. Do not invent statistics, expert quotations or universal outcomes merely to make a paragraph sound persuasive.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to develop a position with reasons, relevant support and a fair response to a counterargument. Builds on: essay focus, contextual evidence and conditional reasoning. Leads to: stronger paragraph structure and balanced formal argument.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: An argumentative essay defends a position through reasons. A claim needs support that bears on it; repeating a preference is not evidence. A counterargument presents a relevant objection, and a response explains how the writer addresses it. A conclusion should follow the discussion rather than introduce an unsupported new case. An argument can be firm without insulting opponents. Do not invent statistics, expert quotations or universal outcomes merely to make a paragraph sound persuasive.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original model: Original model: A school reading club can be useful when it provides structured discussion. Members can compare interpretations and explain their reasons rather than merely exchange answers. Some may object that meetings take time from individual study. This concern matters, so a club should use suitable meeting times and focused tasks. Participation should be purposeful, not compulsory busywork. A well-organised club can therefore complement individual reading, although its value depends on how members use it.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Choose a clear position and outline reasons with examples. Present an objection accurately before answering it. Qualify a claim when the evidence has limits. Check whether the conclusion is supported and whether the reader can distinguish an invented illustration from a verified statistic.

paper_task.prompt: Write an argumentative essay on whether a school club can complement individual study. State a view, develop reasons, address a fair objection and reach a supported conclusion. Label invented examples and do not fabricate statistics.
model: Original model: A school reading club can be useful when it provides structured discussion. Members can compare interpretations and explain their reasons rather than merely exchange answers. Some may object that meetings take time from individual study. This concern matters, so a club should use suitable meeting times and focused tasks. Participation should be purposeful, not compulsory busywork. A well-organised club can therefore complement individual reading, although its value depends on how members use it.
checklist: My position and reasons are clear.
My support is relevant and I address an objection fairly.
My conclusion follows my reasoning and my language remains respectful.
